questions.question: A partnership firm is not registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. Which disability does it suffer?
options: A) Partners cannot share profits among themselves
B) The partnership deed automatically becomes void
C) The firm cannot sue a third party to enforce contractual rights
D) The firm cannot carry on any business
questions.explanation: Under Section 69 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, an unregistered firm cannot file a suit against a third party to enforce a right arising from a contract.

questions.question: Partner Nisha withdrew ₹4,000 on 1st July, ₹7,000 on 1st October, and ₹3,000 on 1st February during the year ending 31st March. Interest on drawings is 9% p.a. Total interest is:
Net profit ₹9,40,000. Interest on capital ₹2,00,000. Salary ₹2,20,000. Commission to Partner B is 10% of net profit after interest on capital but before salary. Profit available for distribution is:
A and B share profits 3:2. They admit C for 1/5 share and guarantee C's profit at not less than ₹1,80,000 p.a. Firm's profit is ₹5,40,000. A's share after guarantee is:

questions.sub_topic: Past Adjustment — Interest on Drawings Omitted
questions.question: In 2024-25, a firm omitted interest on drawings: Partner R ₹4,500, Partner S ₹3,500. Profits were shared equally. The year's profit was ₹2,00,000. What adjustment entry rectifies this?
options: B) Debit R ₹2,000 and S ₹2,000, Credit P&L Adjustment ₹4,000
questions.explanation: If interest on drawings was omitted, profit was understated by ₹8,000 (4,500+3,500). This ₹8,000 should have been distributed equally (₹4,000 each). But R's actual drawings interest = ₹4,500, S's = ₹3,500. R was overpaid by ₹500 (got ₹4,000 but should bear ₹4,500), S was underpaid by ₹500 (got ₹4,000 but should bear only ₹3,500). Adjustment: Debit R's Capital ₹500, Credit S's Capital ₹500.

questions.question: M and N share profits 3:2. In 2024-25, commission to M @ 10% of net profit (before charging commission) was omitted. The net profit was ₹8,00,000. What is the rectifying entry's effect on N's capital?

questions.sub_topic: Fixed vs Fluctuating Capital — Current Account Treatment
questions.question: Under the fixed capital method, a partner's Current Account had a credit balance of ₹45,000 at the start of the year. During the year: salary ₹72,000, interest on capital ₹28,000, share of profit ₹1,15,000, drawings ₹80,000, interest on drawings ₹6,000. What is the Current Account balance at year-end?
questions.explanation: Credit side: Opening ₹45,000 + Salary ₹72,000 + Interest on capital ₹28,000 + Share of profit ₹1,15,000 = ₹2,60,000. Debit side: Drawings ₹80,000 + Interest on drawings ₹6,000 = ₹86,000. Net balance = ₹2,60,000 - ₹86,000 = ₹1,74,000 (Credit).

questions.question: A and B share profits 3:2. They admit C for 1/5 share. C is guaranteed a minimum of ₹1,50,000 p.a., and A alone bears any deficiency. If the firm's profit is ₹4,50,000, what is A's final share?
P and Q share profits 3:2. They admit R for 1/5 share which he acquires from P and Q in the ratio 2:1. The new profit-sharing ratio of P, Q, and R is:
A firm's profits for the last 4 years were ₹2,40,000, ₹3,60,000, ₹4,80,000, and ₹3,00,000. Goodwill is valued at 2 years' purchase of average profit. The value of goodwill is:
A firm earns ₹12,00,000 capital employed with a normal rate of return of 12%. The firm's actual profit is ₹2,10,000. Goodwill is valued at 3 years' purchase of super profit. The value of goodwill is:

A firm's capital employed is ₹15,00,000 and the normal rate of return is 10%. If the firm's average profit is ₹2,00,000, what is the value of goodwill under the capitalisation of average profit method?
questions.explanation: Capitalised value of average profit = ₹2,00,000 / 10% = ₹20,00,000. Capital employed = ₹15,00,000. Goodwill = ₹20,00,000 - ₹15,00,000 = ₹5,00,000.

questions.question: On reconstitution: Building appreciated by ₹3,00,000; Machinery depreciated by ₹1,20,000; Creditors overstated by ₹40,000; Unrecorded liability of ₹60,000 discovered. What is the net effect on Revaluation Account?
questions.explanation: Credit side: Building appreciation ₹3,00,000 + Creditors overstated ₹40,000 = ₹3,40,000. Debit side: Machinery depreciation ₹1,20,000 + Unrecorded liability ₹60,000 = ₹1,80,000. Net profit = ₹3,40,000 - ₹1,80,000 = ₹1,60,000.

questions.question: X and Y share profits 5:3. They admit Z for 1/4 share. Z brings ₹3,00,000 as capital and ₹60,000 as goodwill. The goodwill amount will be shared by X and Y in:
questions.explanation: When a new partner brings goodwill, it is shared by existing partners in their sacrificing ratio. Since Z gets 1/4 share from X and Y in their old ratio (5:3), the sacrificing ratio = old ratio = 5:3. Goodwill ₹60,000 is shared in 5:3 ratio.

questions.question: A, B, C share profits 5:3:2. C retires. Goodwill (not in books) is valued at ₹4,50,000. A and B will share future profits in 3:2 ratio. C's share of goodwill will be debited to A and B in gaining ratio of:
questions.explanation: C's share = 2/10 × ₹4,50,000 = ₹90,000. A's gain = 3/5 - 5/10 = 6/10 - 5/10 = 1/10. B's gain = 2/5 - 3/10 = 4/10 - 3/10 = 1/10. Gaining ratio = 1:1. C's share is debited equally to A and B.

questions.sub_topic: Death of Partner — Profit Share up to Death
questions.question: P, Q, R share profits 4:3:3. R dies on 30th September. The firm's annual profit for the year ending 31st March is ₹12,00,000 (assumed evenly earned). R's estate will receive profit share of:
On reconstitution: Debtors are ₹8,00,000. A provision for doubtful debts @ 5% was already existing. Now it is to be increased to 8%. What is the loss on revaluation for this item?
questions.explanation: Old provision = 5% × ₹8,00,000 = ₹40,000. New provision = 8% × ₹8,00,000 = ₹64,000. Increase in provision = ₹64,000 - ₹40,000 = ₹24,000 (loss on revaluation).

questions.question: On dissolution of a partnership firm, the first step in the settlement of accounts is:
options: B) Distribution of remaining cash to partners
C) Sale of assets and realization of debts
questions.explanation: On dissolution, the first step is to prepare the Realisation Account by transferring all assets (except cash) and all external liabilities to it. This account records the sale of assets and payment of liabilities.

questions.question: On dissolution, assets are transferred to Realisation Account at:
questions.explanation: All assets (except cash and bank balance) are transferred to the Realisation Account at their book value. The actual amount realised on sale may differ from the book value.

questions.question: A firm has assets of ₹10,00,000 and external liabilities of ₹3,00,000. The assets are sold for ₹8,50,000. Partners share profits equally. The loss on realisation to be transferred to partners' capital accounts is:
questions.explanation: Assets sold for ₹8,50,000, book value ₹10,00,000. Loss = ₹10,00,000 - ₹8,50,000 = ₹1,50,000. This loss is distributed equally among partners.

questions.question: On dissolution, Partner A's capital account shows a debit balance of ₹25,000 after sharing loss. Partners B and C share profits 3:2. The deficiency of A will be shared by B and C in:
questions.explanation: When a partner's capital account shows a debit balance (deficiency) on dissolution, the remaining partners share it in their profit-sharing ratio. B and C share in 3:2 ratio.

questions.sub_topic: Realisation Account — Partner's Asset Taken Over
questions.question: On dissolution, Partner B takes over an asset (book value ₹4,50,000) at an agreed value of ₹3,80,000. The correct journal entry is:
options: A) Debit B's Capital ₹3,80,000; Credit Realisation ₹3,80,000
B) Debit Realisation ₹4,50,000; Credit B's Capital ₹4,50,000
C) Debit Realisation ₹3,80,000; Credit B's Capital ₹3,80,000
D) Debit B's Capital ₹4,50,000; Credit Realisation ₹4,50,000
questions.explanation: When a partner takes over an asset, the partner's capital is debited with the agreed value and Realisation Account is credited with the same amount. Journal entry: Debit B's Capital A/c ₹3,80,000; Credit Realisation A/c ₹3,80,000.

questions.question: A, B, C share profits 4:3:3. On dissolution, C is insolvent and cannot pay his capital deficiency of ₹60,000. According to Garner vs Murray rule, this deficiency will be borne by A and B in:
questions.explanation: As per the Garner vs Murray rule, if a partner is insolvent on dissolution, the remaining partners must bring in cash to cover the loss. The insolvent partner's deficiency is shared by solvent partners in their capital ratio (not profit-sharing ratio). If capital ratio is not specified, it's assumed equal.

questions.question: A firm's balance sheet shows: Assets ₹20,00,000; External Liabilities ₹5,00,000; Capital A ₹8,00,000; Capital B ₹7,00,000. Assets sold for ₹17,50,000. Liabilities paid at book value. Partners share profits equally. B's capital balance after settlement is:
questions.explanation: Total capital = ₹8,00,000 + ₹7,00,000 = ₹15,00,000. External liabilities paid = ₹5,00,000. Cash available = ₹17,50,000 - ₹5,00,000 = ₹12,50,000. Total capital payable = ₹15,00,000. Shortfall = ₹2,50,000 (loss on realisation). Each partner's share = ₹2,50,000 / 2 = ₹1,25,000. B's final capital = ₹7,00,000 - ₹1,25,000 = ₹5,75,000.

questions.question: On dissolution of a partnership firm, the correct order of payment is:
options: A) Partner's capital → Partner's loan → External liabilities
B) Partner's loan → External liabilities → Partner's capital
C) External liabilities → Partner's loan → Partner's capital
D) External liabilities → Partner's capital → Partner's loan
questions.explanation: On dissolution, the correct order of payment is: (1) External liabilities (third-party debts), (2) Partner's loan (amount due to partners other than capital), (3) Partner's capital. This is as per Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

questions.question: A company's authorised capital is ₹50,00,000 divided into shares of ₹10 each. The company can issue a maximum of:
questions.explanation: Authorised capital = ₹50,00,000. Face value per share = ₹10. Maximum shares = ₹50,00,000 / ₹10 = 5,00,000 shares.

questions.question: A company received applications for 1,20,000 shares against 80,000 shares issued. Mr. X applied for 12,000 shares. How many shares will be allotted to Mr. X?
questions.explanation: Pro-rata ratio = 80,000 / 1,20,000 = 2/3. Mr. X applied for 12,000 shares. Allotment = 12,000 × 2/3 = 8,000 shares.

questions.question: A share of ₹10 each (₹7 called up) is forfeited. The amount already received on this share is ₹4. What is the amount credited to Share Forfeiture Account?
questions.explanation: When a share is forfeited, the Share Forfeiture Account is credited with the amount already received from the defaulting shareholder. Here, ₹4 was received.

questions.question: A share of ₹10 each (₹6 called up) is forfeited. ₹4 has been received on this share. The share is reissued as fully paid. The maximum discount allowed on reissue is:
questions.explanation: The maximum discount allowed on reissue of forfeited shares is limited to the amount credited to Share Forfeiture Account. Here, ₹4 was received and forfeited, so maximum discount = ₹4 per share.

questions.question: A company issues 1,000 debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 5%. The amount received on issue is:

A company issued 10,000 shares of ₹10 each payable ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment, and ₹3 on first call. A member holding 500 shares failed to pay allotment and first call. The Calls-in-Arrears amount is:
questions.explanation: Allotment arrears = 500 × ₹4 = ₹2,000. First call arrears = 500 × ₹3 = ₹1,500. Total Calls-in-Arrears = ₹3,500.

questions.question: A company has 5,000 debentures of ₹100 each carrying 8% interest. The interest for the year is ₹40,000. If the company pays ₹30,000 interest during the year, what is the outstanding interest at year-end?

questions.sub_topic: Share Forfeiture — Capital Reserve on Reissue
questions.question: 500 shares of ₹10 each are forfeited (₹6 called up, ₹4 received). These shares are reissued at ₹8 per share fully paid. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve is:
questions.explanation: Share Forfeiture Account has ₹4 × 500 = ₹2,000. Reissue at ₹8 (fully paid at ₹10) means discount = ₹2 per share × 500 = ₹1,000. This discount is debited to Share Forfeiture. Balance in Share Forfeiture = ₹2,000 - ₹1,000 = ₹1,000, which is transferred to Capital Reserve.

questions.question: A company issues 2,000 debentures of ₹100 each at a premium of 10%. The total amount received is:
Total debt is ₹20,00,000 and shareholders' equity is ₹30,00,000. The debt-equity ratio is:
questions.explanation: Debt-equity ratio = Total debt / Shareholders' equity = ₹20,00,000 / ₹30,00,000 = 2:3.

questions.question: Sales in 2023-24 were ₹80,00,000 and in 2024-25 are ₹1,00,00,000. The percentage increase in sales is:

Net profit before tax is ₹15,00,000. Depreciation is ₹2,00,000. Loss on sale of asset is ₹50,000. Increase in debtors is ₹1,00,000. Decrease in stock is ₹80,000. The cash flow from operating activities is:
questions.explanation: Operating cash flow = Net profit + Depreciation + Loss on sale - Increase in debtors + Decrease in stock = ₹15,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 + ₹50,000 - ₹1,00,000 + ₹80,000 = ₹17,30,000.

questions.question: Cost of goods sold is ₹24,00,000. Opening stock is ₹4,00,000 and closing stock is ₹8,00,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
questions.explanation: Average stock = (₹4,00,000 + ₹8,00,000) / 2 = ₹6,00,000. Inventory turnover = Cost of goods sold / Average stock = ₹24,00,000 / ₹6,00,000 = 4 times.

questions.question: In a common size balance sheet, total assets are ₹50,00,000. Fixed assets are ₹30,00,000. What percentage of total assets is fixed assets?
A company issues shares worth ₹10,00,000, redeems debentures of ₹4,00,000, and pays dividend of ₹1,00,000. The net cash flow from financing activities is:
questions.explanation: Issue of shares = +₹10,00,000. Redemption of debentures = -₹4,00,000. Dividend paid = -₹1,00,000. Net cash flow from financing = ₹10,00,000 - ₹4,00,000 - ₹1,00,000 = ₹5,00,000.

questions.question: In a spreadsheet, the function used to add a range of cells is:
questions.explanation: The SUM function is used to add a range of cells in a spreadsheet. For example, =SUM(A1:A10) adds cells A1 through A10.

questions.question: In Excel, the function used to calculate depreciation using the straight-line method is:
questions.explanation: The SLN function in Excel calculates straight-line depreciation. Syntax: =SLN(cost, salvage, life). DB uses fixed-declining balance, DDB uses double-declining balance, and VDB uses variable declining balance.

questions.question: In Excel, the PMT function is used to calculate:
options: A) Equal periodic payment for a loan
C) Future value of an investment
D) Present value of an investment
questions.explanation: The PMT function calculates the equal periodic payment for a loan based on constant payments and a constant interest rate. Syntax: =PMT(rate, nper, pv).

questions.question: In Excel, which feature is used to restrict the type of data that can be entered in a cell?
questions.explanation: Data Validation is used to restrict the type of data or the values that users can enter in a cell. For example, you can restrict entries to whole numbers, dates, or a specific list.

questions.question: In Excel, VLOOKUP is used to:
options: A) Calculate the average of a range
B) Count the number of cells that meet a condition
C) Look up a value in the first column and return a value in the same row from another column
D) Look up a value in the first row and return a value in the same column from another row
questions.explanation: VLOOKUP (Vertical Lookup) searches for a value in the first column of a table and returns a value in the same row from a specified column. Syntax: =VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]).

questions.question: A, B, C share profits 5:3:2. On dissolution, C is insolvent. Capital balances: A ₹12,00,000 (Cr), B ₹8,00,000 (Cr), C ₹3,00,000 (Dr). The deficiency of C will be shared by A and B in:
questions.explanation: As per Garner vs Murray rule, an insolvent partner's deficiency is shared by solvent partners in their capital ratio (not profit-sharing ratio). A:B capital ratio = ₹12,00,000:₹8,00,000 = 3:2.

questions.question: A company issues 500 debentures of ₹1,000 each at 95 (i.e., 5% discount) with a premium on redemption of 5%. The total amount to be redeemed is:
questions.explanation: Face value per debenture = ₹1,000. Premium on redemption = 5% × ₹1,000 = ₹50. Total per debenture = ₹1,050. Total for 500 = 500 × ₹1,050 = ₹5,25,000.

questions.question: A company has net profit after tax of ₹18,00,000 and total investment (shareholders' equity + long-term debt) of ₹1,20,00,000. The return on investment ratio is:
questions.explanation: Return on Investment = (Net Profit after Tax / Total Investment) × 100 = (₹18,00,000 / ₹1,20,00,000) × 100 = 15%.

questions.question: In Excel, a Pivot Table is primarily used to:
options: C) Protect data from unauthorized access
D) Summarize and analyze large datasets dynamically
questions.explanation: A Pivot Table is an interactive table that summarizes and analyzes large datasets dynamically. It allows users to rearrange, filter, and aggregate data to reveal patterns and trends.

questions.question: A and B share profits 3:2. C is admitted for 1/5 share and guaranteed ₹1,80,000 p.a. The deficiency is borne by A and B in 3:2 ratio. If the firm's profit is ₹6,00,000, what is B's final share?
questions.explanation: C's actual share = 1/5 × ₹6,00,000 = ₹1,20,000. Deficiency = ₹60,000 borne by A and B in 3:2 ratio. B's share of deficiency = 2/5 × ₹60,000 = ₹24,000. B's normal share = 8/25 × ₹6,00,000 = ₹1,92,000. B's final share = ₹1,92,000 - ₹24,000 = ₹1,68,000.
